meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A government big enough to give you everything you want is a government big enough to take from you everything you have'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Jefferson — no version appears in his writings. The exact wording is Gerald Ford's, 12 Aug 1974. Earliest print: Paul Harvey, 1952, unattributed.

answer.label: Not Thomas Jefferson — the exact line is Gerald Ford’s
answer.sourceLine: This exact wording is documented in President Gerald Ford’s Address to a Joint Session of the Congress on 12 August 1974, his first speech to Congress after Nixon’s resignation — confirmed word-for-word in the official Public Papers. Ford did not coin it, though: the saying was already circulating anonymously in the 1950s, and it has no connection whatsoever to Thomas Jefferson, in whose writings no version of it appears.
answer.confidenceText: The wording is firmly sourced to Ford’s 1974 address; the saying’s ultimate author remains unknown.

source.excerpt: Whether we like it or not, the American wage earner and the American housewife are a lot better economists than most economists care to admit. They know that a government big enough to give you everything you want is a government big enough to take from you everything you have.
source.trailTitle: How a 1950s newspaper filler became a Jefferson quote
trail: 1952 — The earliest known appearance in print, and it names no author at all. Researcher Barry Popik documents it in radio broadcaster Paul Harvey’s Remember These Things (Chicago: Heritage Foundation, 1952), p. 57, in an earlier wording: “If your government is big enough to give you everything you want, it is big enough to take away from you everything you have.” Popik’s citation trail ↗

1957 — Still anonymous, and circulating as a newspaper filler joke. Popik records the Hartford Courant of 31 July 1957 running it on page 1 under “Today’s Chuckle”: “Any government that is big enough to give you everything you want is big enough to take everything you’ve got.” See the 1957 citation ↗

12 August 1974 — President Gerald Ford delivers the wording the internet now quotes, in his first address to a joint session of Congress. The sentence is confirmed verbatim in the transcript. Full text on Wikisource ↗

2005 — Only now, after roughly half a century in circulation and 179 years after Jefferson’s death, does the line turn up in print with his name on it — the earliest known attribution to Jefferson, in Robert G. Moscatelli’s The Quote Manual. Check Your Fact, citing Monticello ↗
source.excerptNote: Ford was addressing Congress three days into his presidency, arguing for restraint on federal spending amid severe inflation. The sentence appears verbatim in the official Public Papers text and in the Wikisource transcription — the popular quotation is not a paraphrase of Ford, it is exactly what he said.

source.rightsNote: The exact wording’s documented source is Ford’s 12 August 1974 address to Congress, delivered as an official act of the President and published in the government’s Public Papers of the Presidents. Works of the U.S. federal government are not subject to copyright under 17 U.S.C. § 105 ↗, so this passage is free to reproduce. Note the separate case of the earliest known printing: Paul Harvey’s Remember These Things (1952) remains in copyright — but it carries a different wording, not the line quoted here.

author.name: Gerald R. Ford
author.heading: About Gerald R. Ford
author.bio: Gerald Ford represented Michigan in the U.S. House for 25 years, rising to House Minority Leader, before becoming Vice President in 1973 and President in August 1974 upon Richard Nixon’s resignation — the only person to have served as both Vice President and President without being elected to either office. His first address to Congress, delivered three days into his presidency amid severe inflation, is where this line enters the historical record in its now-famous form. Ford was a transmitter, not the author: by his own account he picked the saying up early in his political career, and it was already in print before he ever used it.

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on, and why
misattribution.intro: This line has been credited to at least four different figures, and the most famous credit is the only one that is flatly impossible. The saying’s earliest printings name no author, and no attribution ever stuck: by the mid-1950s it was being credited to whichever speaker had just used it — Gerald Ford in 1954, a Kiwanis officer the same year, Ezra Taft Benson by 1963 — which is precisely why famous names kept getting attached to it later.

items.scope: The entire quotation, in every variant
items.why: The attribution is simply false. Monticello’s Jefferson Retirement Series catalogues the line under Spurious Quotes ↗, and its Thomas Jefferson Encyclopedia ↗ states that “neither this quotation nor any of its variant forms has been found in the writings of Thomas Jefferson.” Jefferson died in 1826; the line does not appear in print until 1952, and it is not known to have been printed with his name on it until 2005 ↗. The Jefferson version is the youngest part of the story, not the oldest.

Goldwater is often named as the source, and the line suited his 1964 presidential campaign — Barry Popik notes that some credited the saying’s origin to him ↗. But it was already in print more than a decade before that campaign, so he cannot have coined it.

Eisenhower’s Secretary of Agriculture is the best-documented of the mid-century claimants: Barry Popik records the Los Angeles Times of 7 January 1963 quoting him using the line at a rally, and his 1964 book Title of Liberty (p. 204) elaborating on it. See Popik’s Benson citations ↗ But the same disqualifier applies as to Goldwater: the saying was already in print in 1952, a decade before Benson was ever linked to it. He passed it on; he did not coin it.

Ford genuinely said this exact sentence to Congress on 12 August 1974 — that part is solid. What he did not do is invent it. PolitiFact reports that Ford’s assistant said Ford had picked the phrase up “early in his political career” from Harvard McClain at the Economic Club in Chicago, and that Ford had already used a version of it as a congressman in 1954 ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer has two halves. The wording everyone quotes is Gerald Ford’s, from his 12 August 1974 address to Congress ↗. The saying is older than Ford and belongs to nobody in particular — it surfaces unattributed in 1952 and again as a 1957 newspaper filler joke ↗. What is certain is the negative: it is not Jefferson’s, and never was.

context.heading: Why this one stuck to Jefferson
lead: An anonymous saying is unstable. This line drifted through American print for half a century without ever settling on an owner — a radio host’s aside in 1952, a one-line chuckle on the front page of the Hartford Courant in 1957, an applause line for congressmen and presidential candidates. Names attached readily enough — Ford in 1954, Ezra Taft Benson by 1963 — but always to whoever had just said it out loud, and none of them held. Sayings in that condition tend to get adopted, and the name they attract is rarely the name of whoever actually thought of them. It is the name that makes the sentiment sound most authoritative.

Jefferson is the natural magnet. The line is an epigram about the danger of concentrated government power, which is recognisably Jeffersonian in theme — and that thematic fit is exactly what makes the misattribution so durable. It feels right, so nobody checks. But feeling Jeffersonian and being Jefferson are different claims, and the documentary record only supports the first. The irony is that the line already had a perfectly good, fully documented American source: a sitting president, on the record, before a joint session of Congress, in a speech anyone can read.
detailsBody: A note on the “sequel” sentence. The quotation is sometimes extended with a second line: “The course of history shows that as a government grows, liberty decreases.” This too is not Jefferson’s wording. Monticello treats it as a likely garbling of something Jefferson did write — “The natural progress of things is for liberty to yeild, and government to gain ground” — which is a real Jefferson sentence but a different thought, and not a continuation of the government-big-enough line.

Why 1952 is a floor, not a birthdate. Barry Popik’s 1952 citation is the earliest known printing, not necessarily the first utterance. It appears in Paul Harvey’s book without attribution and without any framing that presents it as new or as Harvey’s own, which is usually a sign that a saying is already in circulation. The true origin may well be older and oral — and may never be recoverable.
context.pull: The line spent fifty years with no author. Then it got the most famous one available.
